summary.text: Twice integrating by parts shows that \(K_r=\int_0^1 e^x(x(1-x))^r\,dx\) satisfies \(K_r=r(r-1)K_{r-2}-2r(2r-1)K_{r-1}\); after signed factorial normalization this is the same recurrence and has the same initial values as the odd-index errors \(b(2m+1)e-a(2m+1)\), while \(0\le K_r\le e\) gives factorial decay of those errors. An algebraic bridge expresses each even-index error as a linear combination of two neighboring odd errors (whose factorial decay dominates the linear coefficient), and positivity of all corresponding denominators then yields convergence of both parity subsequences, hence of the full ratio sequence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 A_n=A340737(n),\qquad B_n=A340738(n),
\]
where the two sequences obey the same recurrence but have initial values
\[
(A_1,A_2)=(3,5),\qquad (B_1,B_2)=(1,2).
\]
Thus, for odd \(n>2\),
\[
 X_n=2X_{n-1}+nX_{n-2},                                      \tag{1}
\]
and for even \(n>2\),
\[
 X_n=\frac{n+2}{2}X_{n-1}-X_{n-2}-\frac{n-2}{2}X_{n-3},       \tag{2}
\]
where \(X\) can mean either \(A\) or \(B\). We will prove that
\[
 \frac{A_n}{B_n}\longrightarrow e=\exp(1).
\]
The value assigned at index \(0\) is irrelevant to this limit.

First we simplify the mixed recurrence by separating odd and even indices.

For either sequence \(X\), the odd recurrence gives, for every \(m\geq 0\),
\[
 X_{2m+3}=2X_{2m+2}+(2m+3)X_{2m+1}.                           \tag{3}
\]
We also have the following bridge from an even term to neighboring odd terms:
\[
 2X_{2m+2}=(2m+3)X_{2m+1}+P_X(m),                             \tag{4}
\]
where
\[
 P_A(0)=P_B(0)=1,
\]
and, for \(m\geq1\),
\[
 P_A(m)=A_{2m-1},\qquad P_B(m)=B_{2m-1}.
\]
For \(m=0\), this is an immediate check from the initial values:
\[
2A_2=10=3A_1+1,
\qquad
2B_2=4=3B_1+1.
\]
For the remaining cases, write the even index as \(2m+4\), with \(m\geq0\). The expression on the right side of the even recurrence is
\[
 z=(m+3)X_{2m+3}-X_{2m+2}-(m+1)X_{2m+1}.
\]
Using (3), or equivalently
\[
 2X_{2m+2}=X_{2m+3}-(2m+3)X_{2m+1},
\]
we calculate
\[
\begin{aligned}
2z
 &=2(m+3)X_{2m+3}-2X_{2m+2}-2(m+1)X_{2m+1}\\
 &=2(m+3)X_{2m+3}-\bigl(X_{2m+3}-(2m+3)X_{2m+1}\bigr)
      -2(m+1)X_{2m+1}\\
 &=(2m+5)X_{2m+3}+X_{2m+1}.                                  \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
The last expression is nonnegative. In particular, even if the sequence definition is viewed as taking the nonnegative part of the integer subtraction in (2), no truncation occurs: \(z\geq0\), so \(X_{2m+4}=z\). Equation (5) is therefore
\[
 2X_{2m+4}=(2m+5)X_{2m+3}+X_{2m+1},
\]
which is exactly (4) with \(m\) replaced by \(m+1\).

Combining the bridge with the next odd step yields a recurrence involving only odd-indexed terms. Indeed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
X_{2m+5}
 &=2X_{2m+4}+(2m+5)X_{2m+3}\\
 &=\bigl((2m+5)X_{2m+3}+X_{2m+1}\bigr)
      +(2m+5)X_{2m+3}\\
 &=(4m+10)X_{2m+3}+X_{2m+1}.                                 \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the odd subsequences of both \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy the same second-order recurrence.

We next construct an analytic sequence satisfying this same recurrence. For every integer \(r\geq0\), put
\[
 K_r=\int_0^1 e^x\bigl(x(1-x)\bigr)^r\,dx.                    \tag{7}
\]
We need a recurrence for these integrals. Let
\[
 \phi_r(x)=\bigl(x(1-x)\bigr)^r.
\]
For \(r\geq2\), both \(\phi_r\) and \(\phi_r'\) vanish at \(0\) and \(1\). Two integrations by parts therefore give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \int_0^1 e^x\phi_r''(x)\,dx
 &=\bigl[e^x\phi_r'(x)\bigr]_0^1-
       \int_0^1 e^x\phi_r'(x)\,dx\\
 &=-\left(\bigl[e^x\phi_r(x)\bigr]_0^1-
       \int_0^1 e^x\phi_r(x)\,dx\right)\\
 &=K_r.                                                       \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
A direct differentiation gives
\[
 \phi_r'(x)=r\bigl(x(1-x)\bigr)^{r-1}(1-2x).
\]
Differentiating once more and using
\[
 (1-2x)^2=1-4x(1-x)
\]
yields
\[
 \phi_r''(x)
 =r(r-1)\bigl(x(1-x)\bigr)^{r-2}
  -2r(2r-1)\bigl(x(1-x)\bigr)^{r-1}.                         \tag{9}
\]
Substituting (9) into (8) gives, for every \(r\geq2\),
\[
 K_r=r(r-1)K_{r-2}-2r(2r-1)K_{r-1}.                           \tag{10}
\]

Define
\[
 S_m=\frac{(-1)^{m+1}K_{m+1}}{(m+1)!}\qquad(m\geq0).          \tag{11}
\]
Apply (10) with \(r=m+3\):
\[
 K_{m+3}=(m+3)(m+2)K_{m+1}
          -2(m+3)(2m+5)K_{m+2}.
\]
After multiplying by \((-1)^{m+3}/(m+3)!\), the first term becomes \(S_m\), and the second becomes \((4m+10)S_{m+1}\). Hence
\[
 S_{m+2}=(4m+10)S_{m+1}+S_m.                                 \tag{12}
\]
This is exactly the recurrence (6) satisfied by linear combinations of the odd subsequences.

We now compute the first two values of \(S_m\). First,
\[
 K_0=\int_0^1e^x\,dx=e-1.                                    \tag{13}
\]
Also,
\[
 K_1=\int_0^1e^x x(1-x)\,dx=3-e.                             \tag{14}
\]
For example, an antiderivative of the integrand in (14) is
\[
 e^x(-x^2+3x-3),
\]
as is checked by differentiation; evaluating it at \(1\) and \(0\) gives \(-e-(-3)=3-e\). Taking \(r=2\) in (10) and using (13) and (14), we obtain
\[
 K_2=2K_0-12K_1
    =2(e-1)-12(3-e)
    =14e-38.                                                   \tag{15}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 S_0=-K_1=e-3,                                                 \tag{16}
\]
and
\[
 S_1=\frac{K_2}{2!}=7e-19.                                    \tag{17}
\]

Consider now the errors on the odd-indexed fractions:
\[
 E_m^{\mathrm{odd}}=B_{2m+1}e-A_{2m+1}.                       \tag{18}
\]
Because both \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy (6), their linear combination (18) satisfies
\[
 E_{m+2}^{\mathrm{odd}}
  =(4m+10)E_{m+1}^{\mathrm{odd}}+E_m^{\mathrm{odd}}.           \tag{19}
\]
The initial terms are
\[
 E_0^{\mathrm{odd}}=B_1e-A_1=e-3=S_0.
\]
The odd recurrence gives \(A_3=2A_2+3A_1=19\) and
\(B_3=2B_2+3B_1=7\), so
\[
 E_1^{\mathrm{odd}}=7e-19=S_1.
\]
Equations (12) and (19), together with these two initial equalities, imply by induction that
\[
 E_m^{\mathrm{odd}}=S_m
 =\frac{(-1)^{m+1}K_{m+1}}{(m+1)!}                            \tag{20}
\]
for every \(m\geq0\).

The integral representation gives a simple uniform bound. On \([0,1]\),
\[
 0\leq x(1-x)\leq1,
 \qquad 0<e^x\leq e.
\]
Therefore the integrand in (7) is nonnegative and at most \(e\), and the interval has length \(1\). Thus
\[
 0\leq K_r\leq e                                               \tag{21}
\]
for all \(r\geq0\). From (20),
\[
 \left|E_m^{\mathrm{odd}}\right|
 \leq \frac{e}{(m+1)!}\longrightarrow0.                      \tag{22}
\]

We also need positivity of the denominators. Let
\[
 q_m=B_{2m+1}.
\]
We have \(q_0=B_1=1>0\) and \(q_1=B_3=7>0\). By (6),
\[
 q_{m+2}=(4m+10)q_{m+1}+q_m,
\]
so induction shows that every \(q_m\) is a positive integer. Hence
\[
 B_{2m+1}\geq1.                                                \tag{23}
\]
Now
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac{A_{2m+1}}{B_{2m+1}}-e
 &=\frac{A_{2m+1}-B_{2m+1}e}{B_{2m+1}}\\
 &=-\frac{E_m^{\mathrm{odd}}}{B_{2m+1}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using (23) and then (22),
\[
 \left|\frac{A_{2m+1}}{B_{2m+1}}-e\right|
 \leq \left|E_m^{\mathrm{odd}}\right|
 \leq \frac{e}{(m+1)!}\longrightarrow0.                     \tag{24}
\]
Thus the odd-indexed fractions converge to \(e\).

It remains to treat the even-indexed fractions. Define
\[
 E_m^{\mathrm{even}}=B_{2m+2}e-A_{2m+2}.                      \tag{25}
\]
Apply the bridge identity (4) to \(A\) and \(B\) at index \(m+1\):
\[
 2A_{2m+4}=(2m+5)A_{2m+3}+A_{2m+1},
\]
\[
 2B_{2m+4}=(2m+5)B_{2m+3}+B_{2m+1}.
\]
Multiply the second equation by \(e\), subtract the first, and use (18) and (25). This gives
\[
 2E_{m+1}^{\mathrm{even}}
  =(2m+5)E_{m+1}^{\mathrm{odd}}+E_m^{\mathrm{odd}}.            \tag{26}
\]
Both terms on the right tend to zero. The second does so by (22). For the first, (22) gives
\[
 \left|(2m+5)E_{m+1}^{\mathrm{odd}}\right|
 \leq \frac{e(2m+5)}{(m+2)!}.
\]
This upper bound tends to zero. For instance,
\[
 \frac{2m+5}{(m+2)!}
 =\frac{2m+5}{m+2}\cdot\frac1{(m+1)!}
 \leq \frac{3}{(m+1)!},                                      \tag{27}
\]
since \(2m+5\leq3(m+2)\). Hence (26) implies
\[
 E_{m+1}^{\mathrm{even}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Removing or adding the single initial term does not affect a limit, so
\[
 E_m^{\mathrm{even}}\longrightarrow0.                         \tag{28}
\]

The even denominators are positive as well. In the bridge identity for \(B\),
\[
 2B_{2m+2}=(2m+3)B_{2m+1}+P_B(m).
\]
We already know that \(B_{2m+1}>0\). Moreover, \(P_B(0)=1>0\), while for \(m\geq1\), \(P_B(m)=B_{2m-1}>0\), again by positivity of the odd subsequence. Thus the right side is positive, and consequently
\[
 B_{2m+2}>0,
 \qquad B_{2m+2}\geq1.                                       \tag{29}
\]
As in the odd case,
\[
 \frac{A_{2m+2}}{B_{2m+2}}-e
 =-\frac{E_m^{\mathrm{even}}}{B_{2m+2}}.
\]
Using (29),
\[
 \left|\frac{A_{2m+2}}{B_{2m+2}}-e\right|
 \leq |E_m^{\mathrm{even}}|\longrightarrow0                  \tag{30}
\]
by (28). Therefore the even-indexed fractions also converge to \(e\).

Finally, the two parity limits imply the limit of the full sequence. Explicitly, let \(\varepsilon>0\). By (24), choose \(M_o\) such that
\[
 m\geq M_o\implies
 \left|\frac{A_{2m+1}}{B_{2m+1}}-e\right|<\varepsilon.
\]
By (30), choose \(M_e\) such that
\[
 m\geq M_e\implies
 \left|\frac{A_{2m+2}}{B_{2m+2}}-e\right|<\varepsilon.
\]
If
\[
 n\geq N:=\max(2M_o+1,\,2M_e+2),
\]
then either \(n\) is odd, in which case \(n=2m+1\) with \(m\geq M_o\), or \(n\) is positive and even, in which case \(n=2m+2\) with \(m\geq M_e\). In either case,
\[
 \left|\frac{A_n}{B_n}-e\right|<\varepsilon.
\]
It follows that
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{A340737(n)}{A340738(n)}=e}.
\]
